newsitem.title: FRANCE: Kohl's reelection bid welcome news in France.
newsitem.headline: Kohl's reelection bid welcome news in France.

text.p: French politicians and analysts hailed on Friday German Chancellor Helmut Kohl's decision to seek an unprecedented fifth term in office as excellent news for Europe and France.

But some French analysts questioned whether Bonn's longest serving post-war leader, beset by record unemployment and public hostility to a single European currency, could win an outright victory in next year's general election.

"Mr Kohl's new candidacy reassures supporters of Europe," the newspaper Le Monde said in its main headline on Friday, summing up widespread relief in Paris that the most Francophile of German politicians planned to stay at the helm.

"Kohl is candidate in 1998 to make a success of Europe," the financial daily Les Echos proclaimed, saying the Christian Democratic leader's decision guaranteed that Germany would enter the planned single European currency on time in 1999.

Pierre Lellouche, a foreign policy expert in President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party, said the continuation of the Kohl-Chirac partnership was the best guarantee of stability and progress in European integration.

In 14 years in office, Kohl has built close partnerships first with the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand and later with Chirac, making the Franco-German relationship the motor of European unification.
Chirac made clear his own delight at Thursday's announcement by issuing a birthday message praising Kohl's "determined action" and wishing him success in all his endeavours.

"It is a great pleasure for me to work with you for progress in Franco-German cooperation, which we both want to make ever stronger, particularly to continue the construction of Europe," the French leader said.
His office announced that the two men would meet in Bonn on Wednesday evening for the latest of their regular informal consultations on European and NATO reform.
Sources close to Chirac said Kohl's decision to run again came as no surprise, and the president, a fellow conservative, fully expected him to win.
They said France considers Kohl the strongest guarantor of European economic and monetary union and his announcement was a clear sign the project will go ahead on time in January 1999.

Alfred Grosser, a veteran French expert on Germany, told Reuters he believed the chancellor alone had the reassuring power to persuade sceptical Germans to abandon the deutschemark in favour of a single European currency.

"Monetary union is deeply unpopular in Germany. That is why Kohl is staying on, precisely because in the election campaign he can push through acceptance of the single currency and achieve his European dream," Grosser said.
He said Kohl's best hope of victory was that the opposition Social Democratic Party (SPD) was deeply split, lacked economic credibility and had no natural coalition partner.
But the Christian Democrats (CDU/CSU) might fall short of a working majority with their Free Democratic (FDP) partners and have to form a grand coalition with the SPD, Grosser said.

Anne-Marie Le Gloannec, a researcher on Germany at Paris's CERI international affairs think-tank, said Kohl's aim was finally to anchor his reunited country in the European Union by achieving monetary union before he stepped down, perhaps two years after the election.
"For the euro to succeed, it will require great political skill. Who else but Kohl can achieve that?" she told the daily Le Figaro.
Le Gloannec said Germans were tired of Kohl, but no one else had a comparable stature.
